title: Gaining the Attention of Someone Who Repeatedly Rejects Your Advocacy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This brief piece argues that when conventional persuasion fails against a committed resister, the most effective tool is changing the physical setting of the conversation rather than changing the message or channel. An unusual setting — a walk, an early breakfast, a park bench, a golf course — signals that something important and different is happening, causing people to listen differently. The change of environment disrupts the automatic refutation response that entrenched people use when familiar topics arise in familiar places. This technique is effective across professional and personal contexts, from resistant clients to children. The new setting does not make the argument for you, but it creates space for the other person to hear it for the first time.
points: When advocacy repeatedly fails to penetrate, changing the physical setting of the conversation is more effective than changing the message or delivery channel.
An unexpected setting — a walk, breakfast, a park bench — signals something important and different is happening, prompting different listening.
Familiar settings trigger automatic resistance; unfamiliar settings disrupt the refutation response and create receptivity.
The technique works in professional contexts with resistant clients and equally well in personal contexts with children.
A new setting does not argue the point — it clears space for the other person to finally hear the argument.
quotes: Strong advocates drastically change the setting for the discussion.
Changing the setting for the discussion almost always gets people to pause, take notice, and process information differently.
They listen differently because the new setting takes them out of their comfort zone and suggests you are treating the conversation as important and distinctive.
When words alone can't break through, changing the room can.
A new setting doesn't argue the point for you, but it clears space for the other person to finally hear your arguments — perhaps for the first time.
